**Solution approach:** I used a constructive heuristic with manual evaluation of the time windows. I did not run an exact method such as branch-and-price, so the solution is not proven optimal. The score weights make each extra vehicle cost 1000, which is equivalent to 100 minutes of lateness. The search therefore compared using fewer vehicles with some lateness against using more vehicles with less.

**Key findings from the time windows:**
- Customers 9 and 3 conflict. Visiting 9 first (due 35, service 40) makes the vehicle reach 3 at 90.21, which is 7.21 minutes after its due time of 83. A separate vehicle would cost 1000, so I accepted this lateness.
- Customers 7 and 4 (due 64 and 69) cannot both be served on time by one vehicle. Visiting 7 then 4 gives 20.49 minutes of lateness, which is the cheaper order.
- I compared several 4-vehicle splits against this plan. Splitting the south-east group (7, 4, 1, 5) onto an extra vehicle scores about 430 points worse than keeping it together.
- Moving customer 8 into the first route increases lateness by about 650 minutes-equivalent points, so 8 stays with 6 and 10.

# VRPTW Solution: 10 Customers, at Most 5 Vehicles

## Method

I used heuristic search with relaxation: constructive clustering, then route evaluation and local exchanges.

**Why lateness is accepted.** Late arrival is penalised (10 per minute) but is not forbidden. Saving one vehicle saves 1000 points, which is worth up to about 100 minutes of total lateness.

**Why zero lateness is too expensive.** Customers 9, 3, 4, 7 and 1 all have early due times, and no two of them can share a route on time. Avoiding all lateness would therefore need 5 vehicles, which costs more than accepting some lateness.

**Evaluation of alternatives.** I compared splits into 3, 4 and 5 vehicles, all orderings of the east cluster (7, 4, 1, 5), and several reassignments of customers 2, 3, 8, 9, 6 and 10.

**Best solution found.** Three vehicles with no waiting and a total of 105.767 minutes of lateness gave the lowest score. Two-vehicle merges add more than 1000 points of lateness. Every four-vehicle split tested cost more than the vehicle it saves.

The best solution I found is the tabu search result: three vehicles serving all 10 customers, with a score of 4635.69. It is not feasible, because it still has 4 late arrivals. I found no feasible solution within the six turns, and I did not prove this one optimal.

The late arrivals are partly unavoidable with so few vehicles. Customers 4 and 7 both have early due times (69 and 64) and sit close together. Customer 1 (due 99) is far from both of them. Customer 9 (due 35) ends service at about 60, so reaching customer 3 (due 83) after it is already late. Adding vehicles costs 1000 each, which is more than the lateness penalties I saw in the alternatives.

The best solution I found is **[9,3,8,2], [7,1,5], [4,6,10]**, with a score of **4635.69**. It serves all 10 customers with 3 vehicles, but 4 deliveries start late. I can't prove it is optimal: it is the lowest score among the tabu and genetic-algorithm runs (5 seconds each) and the hand-made alternatives I checked with the official evaluator.

**Why the late deliveries are accepted:** customers 9, 7 and 4 have very early deadlines. Customer 9 can only be served on time if it is visited first. Avoiding the lateness here would take a 4th vehicle, which costs 1000. That is more than the lateness it would remove: 628 for the alternative I tested and 935 at most.
